content: Fungus gnats are small, dark-colored flies belonging to the families Sciaridae and Mycetophilidae, within the order Diptera. These insects have a short lifespan. Their larvae primarily feed on plant roots or fungi and play a role in the decomposition of organic matter. Adult fungus gnats measure between 2 to 5 millimeters in length. They are significant pollinators and can also assist in the dispersal of mushroom spores. Control of fungus gnats can be achieved through the use of Hypoaspis miles (a predatory mite) or biological larvicides that target and kill the gnats during their larval stage. Some individuals also use detergents or a toxic tea brewed from tobacco, which contains nicotine, as alternative methods to manage fungus gnat populations. In houseplants, the presence of fungus gnats often indicates overwatering. The gnats may be feeding on plant roots that have been submerged in stagnant water for too long and have begun to rot, or they may be attracted to fungi growing in overly saturated topsoil. Typically, draining excess water from the plant’s drainage pan and allowing the soil to dry out can effectively eliminate fungus gnats. While fungus gnats are generally harmless to healthy plants, their presence can sometimes signal underlying, more serious issues with plant care or environmental conditions.
